planting.note: Direct sow into well-drained, sandy soil in spring; fall dormant seeding also works. Stands are fire-adapted and flower and set viable seed most reliably on sites that see periodic burns.

directions: Lopsided indiangrass is a warm-season bunchgrass of the southeastern Coastal Plain, found from Florida into the Carolinas, Gulf states, and Texas on well-drained sandhill and flatwoods sites. It gets its name from the showy, one-sided golden panicle that hangs from the tall flowering stalk in late summer and fall. Plant in lean, well-drained, acidic sandy soil in full sun; this species declines on heavy or poorly drained ground. It is a larval host for the Delaware skipper, dusted skipper, and swarthy skipper butterflies, and benefits from occasional fire or mowing to maintain vigor and seed set.

planting.note: Fall-sow to allow natural cold stratification, or plant plugs in spring into part-shade woodland edges; this species tolerates more shade and dappled light than open-prairie Indiangrass relatives.

directions: Slender Indiangrass ranges from Maryland south to Florida and west through Texas, Tennessee, Arkansas, and Oklahoma, where it is found in oak-hickory woodlands, river-scour bluffs, and over mafic rock outcrops rather than open prairie. It is a finer-textured, more shade-tolerant relative of the familiar prairie Indiangrass, flowering from September through November with slender, less showy panicles. Plant in well-drained woodland or woodland-edge soil in partial sun and allow it to naturalize among native understory species; it requires little care once established and provides late-season cover and seed for wildlife.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in spring; established clumps tolerate periodic dormant-season fire, which maintains open pine-savanna habitat conditions this grass prefers.

directions: Slender bluestem is a wiry, fine-leaved little bluestem relative of the Coastal Plain, ranging from North Carolina across the Florida panhandle to east Texas in longleaf pine savannas, sandhills, and flatwoods. Its slender, leaning stems and narrow wiry leaves give a softer, airier texture than the familiar Schizachyrium scoparium, making it a good textural companion for other pine-savanna wildflowers. Grow in dry, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; it performs poorly in rich or heavy garden soil and is best suited to naturalistic sandhill or pine-savanna restoration plantings. Leave standing through winter for seed and cover, then cut back or burn in late winter before spring growth resumes.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow after soil has warmed following summer monsoon-type rains; this desert annual germinates opportunistically with warm-season moisture and completes its life cycle quickly.

directions: Needle grama is a delicate warm-season annual of the Sonoran and Mojave deserts, native to southern California, Arizona, and northern Mexico on dry, open rocky slopes and washes. Its narrow, awn-tipped florets give the seed head its needle-like appearance, and the whole plant flushes abundantly after summer rains before setting seed and drying down. Scatter seed over open, well-drained mineral soil in full sun; it needs no supplemental care beyond occasional water during establishment and reseeds readily where soil is left undisturbed. Use it for erosion control, desert restoration, or as an authentic textural filler in a low desert native planting.

planting.note: Direct sow or set plugs after the soil has warmed in spring into shallow, rocky, well-drained soil; established plants are extremely drought and heat tolerant but need regular watering the first season.

directions: Sprucetop grama is a small, drought-tolerant bunchgrass native to the desert foothills of southern Arizona and northern Mexico, east to western Texas, found on dry rocky slopes and fine-textured desert grassland soils from about 2,500 to 6,000 feet elevation. Mostly basal, mildly furrowed leaves form a low, spruce-like tuft, and flower spikes with bright orange anthers appear in July and August. Plant in shallow, rocky, acidic clay or gravelly soil in full sun; it is extremely cold hardy and heat tolerant once established, and under good conditions can form a dense, turf-like cover. Use for xeric lawns, desert grassland restoration, or rock-garden plantings where little supplemental water is available.

planting.note: Scatter seed onto open mineral soil after warm-season rains; true to its name, this annual can complete germination-to-seed in about six weeks under good moisture.

directions: Six-weeks grama is a small warm-season annual bunchgrass of the Colorado, Mojave, and Sonoran deserts, found across the southwestern United States into southern Mexico in desert shrubland, desert grassland, and disturbed roadside soils. Comb-like seedhead branches and a low, spreading or semi-erect tuft of stems let it carpet open ground quickly after summer monsoon rain. Sow directly onto bare, well-drained soil in full sun; no transplanting is practical given its short, rapid life cycle. It is valuable for quick erosion control and as forage and cover on disturbed desert ground, reseeding itself freely where left undisturbed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow or install plugs into consistently moist, loamy sand in a fire-maintained or regularly mown wet pineland setting; this species needs sustained soil moisture and does poorly if allowed to dry out completely.

directions: Pinewoods bluestem, also called Florida bluestem, is a perennial grass endemic to Florida and a small part of Alabama, restricted to wet pine flatwoods, pineland bogs, and savanna communities with dry-to-wet loamy sand. It is state-listed as threatened in Florida, so plant only nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected material. Distinctive paired or tripled white, densely hairy flowering racemes appear from August through October atop stems reaching about five feet. Site it in full sun with consistently damp, loamy sand, ideally in a seasonally wet pine-savanna or bog-garden setting that can be periodically burned or mown to suppress woody competition.
sources: Florida Natural Areas Inventory (FNAI) Field Guide

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring into deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun; Henry is a late-ripening selection whose nuts tend to be retained in the husk longer than most shellbark cultivars.

directions: Henry is a historic named shellbark hickory selection made by Fayette Etter of Franklin County, Pennsylvania, prized for annual productivity and very large, well-filled nuts that crack out relatively well for the species. Like other shellbark hickories it is suited to colder northern growing areas and performs best in deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soil where its long taproot can develop undisturbed. Expect a long juvenile period of a decade or more before a grafted tree bears its first crop, and plan for cross-pollination with another shellbark or shagbark hickory to maximize nut set.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring into deep, well-drained soil; Beckwith is protogynous and a late pollinizer, so pair it with an early-pollen butternut or butternut-heartnut hybrid for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Beckwith is a butternut selection noted as one of the most regular annual croppers among named butternut cultivars, producing medium-sized nuts whose kernels crack out in halves and extract easily from the shell. Butternut is now a globally threatened species due to butternut canker disease, so Beckwith and other surviving named selections are valued both for orchard nut production and for conservation grafting and breeding programs working to preserve disease-tolerant genetics. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun away from vegetable beds, since butternut shares black walnut's juglone sensitivity issue for many companion plants, and monitor trunk and limbs for canker symptoms.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring into deep, well-drained soil; pair with a second butternut cultivar with overlapping bloom for best nut set.

directions: Chamberlin is a hardy, productive butternut selection originating near Chamberlain Corners in northern New York, grown for medium-sized nuts with good flavor and easy cracking qualities. It is maintained today mainly through specialty nut nurseries and conservation grafting collections working to preserve surviving butternut genetics against the spread of butternut canker disease. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with room for a large shade canopy at maturity, and expect several years of establishment before the tree reaches bearing age. Harvest nuts promptly when the husks soften in fall, since butternut hulls stain hands and surfaces and nuts left on wet ground mold quickly.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in late winter into deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun; hicans need a nearby pecan or hickory with compatible bloom timing to set a crop, and bearing can be inconsistent.

directions: Rockville is an early-twentieth-century natural hican (pecan x shellbark hickory, Carya x nussbaumeri) discovered in Rockville, Missouri, producing a large nut resembling the old 'Burlington' hican but filling somewhat better. It has long been kept in cultivation mainly by nut-collector grafting rather than commercial orchards, and modern growers generally regard it as an interesting historic selection rather than a dependable producer, since bearing tends to be light and inconsistent compared with modern pecan cultivars. Give it the same deep, well-drained orchard conditions used for pecan and shellbark hickory, plan on a long juvenile period before first nuts, and treat it as a collector or breeding-program tree rather than a reliable home-orchard choice.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Society of Ontario Nut Growers (SONG) News
USDA ARS Pecan Breeding Program hickory cultivar list

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant into deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; a nearby pecan or shellbark hickory is needed for pollination, and northern-grown trees are more reliable as ornamentals than as consistent nut producers.

directions: Gerardi (sometimes spelled Girardi) is a hican cultivar from Damiansville, Illinois, a natural hybrid of pecan and shellbark hickory grown today mainly by nut-tree collectors and occasionally used as rootstock for grafted pecans. It produces strikingly large nuts and grows into a hardy, attractive shade tree, but in northern climates it is a poor and unreliable kernel producer compared with true pecan or hickory selections, making it better suited to ornamental or breeding use than to a home nut orchard. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, give it ample room to mature into a large shade tree, and do not expect dependable annual nut crops.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Society of Ontario Nut Growers (SONG) News

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Porter is a good pollinizer for other shagbark hickory cultivars and bears a mid-season crop.

directions: Porter was introduced from a tree on the Porter farm in Mackeyville, Pennsylvania, around 1960, and went on to win a Pennsylvania Nut Growers Association cracking contest for its combination of good cracking quality and sweet flavor. It is a medium-sized, mid-season-ripening nut on a good-producing tree that also serves as a reliable pollinizer for other shagbark hickory selections. Plant grafted trees into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, water well during establishment, and expect the tree to begin bearing within about five to seven years, considerably sooner than an unimproved seedling.
sources: Society of Ontario Nut Growers (SONG) News
Growing Fruit forum hickory named-selections thread

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Wilcox ripens early and is well suited to colder growing regions.

directions: Wilcox was first discovered as a wild tree near Geneva, Ohio, in 1934 and has since become one of the more widely grafted shagbark hickory cultivars for cold-climate growers. It produces a tasty, medium-sized nut that cracks easily into clean halves, ripens earlier than many shagbark selections, and bears prolifically, with grafted trees reaching bearing age in as little as five to seven years. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a second shagbark hickory nearby for cross-pollination, and protect the young trunk from mower and trimmer damage while the tree establishes its root system.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Society of Ontario Nut Growers (SONG) News
Growing Fruit forum hickory named-selections thread
